title: Why suffering
hook: the Gurus call pain a medicine and never pretend it isn't pain

segments.voice: Yesterday, jug: the ages the Granth uses as a frame for things falling apart and being made new. Your line was ages turn. Did you spot something in decline, and something being renewed? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-two.

A man has been carrying something heavy for a long time, and he's sure the weight is his alone. Everyone else seems fine. Their doors look calm, their windows bright. So he climbs up high, high enough to see the whole town at once. And from up there, he sees it. Smoke from this house. Smoke from that one. House after house, a fire burning inside. That climb isn't a modern story. It's a couplet of Sheikh Farid, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib. Today: why suffering, and what the Gurus say about it.
screen: `ONE MAN, ONE WEIGHT, ONE CLIMB.` → `SMOKE FROM EVERY HOUSE.` → `WHY SUFFERING.`

segments.voice: First, Farid up high. In paraphrase: Farid, I thought the pain was mine alone, but pain is spread through the whole world; when I climbed up and looked, I saw this same fire in house after house. Notice what the couplet doesn't do. It doesn't say the fire is small, or fake, or deserved. It says it's everywhere. That's the starting point: honesty. Second, a line from Guru Nanak in Asa di Var that sounds upside down. In the original: dukh daaroo, sukh rog bhaiaa. Pain became the medicine, and comfort became the disease. Why? The line goes on, in paraphrase: when there is comfort, the Lord is not remembered. Comfort lulls. Pain wakes. When everything is easy, a person can drift a long time without once asking what matters. A hard week can ask that question in an afternoon. Third, and this matters: a medicine is still bitter. Calling pain a medicine is not calling it sweet. The Guru doesn't say it doesn't hurt. Nobody hands someone a bitter cup and says, this is delicious. They say, this is hard, and it may heal. The Gurus' hymns hold real grief, real protest, real crying out; we heard one of those protests last week. Fourth, the medicine is for your own pain, not a verdict on someone else's. A Sikh can say of their own hard season, this woke me up. That's very different from telling a grieving neighbor their loss is good for them. Sikh life answers other people's pain the plain way: with food, with seva, with showing up. So the Gurus give no tidy answer to why. What they give is a way to stand in it: name the fire honestly, let it wake you, and don't leave anyone else alone with their fire.
screen: `FARID: A FIRE IN EVERY HOUSE.` · `PAIN THE MEDICINE, COMFORT THE DISEASE.` · `A MEDICINE IS STILL BITTER.` · `YOUR PAIN, NOT A VERDICT ON THEIRS.` · then, large: `DUKH DAAROO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with one pain honestly. Settle, and breathe. Let one real pain come to mind. Not the biggest one; one you can hold for two minutes. A worry, an ache, a loss. Don't argue with it. Don't tell it that it's fine. Just name it, plainly, in a few words, the way Farid named his fire. Then, gently, ask one question: is this waking anything up in me? If nothing comes, that's all right too. If you pray, you can hold it before God without dressing it up. The bell holds the time.
Why suffering. The Gurus call pain a medicine, because it wakes us when comfort lulls us, and they never pretend it isn't pain. Today's word.

Your line: pain, honestly. Today, when someone asks how you are, give one true answer instead of fine. And if someone gives you a true answer, stay with them a minute. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs often meet hardship by turning to the Guru's word, saying Ardas with family and sangat, and serving others; Guru Nanak's line calling pain the medicine is often recalled in hard times.

original.note: Gurmukhi: pain, the medicine. Guru Nanak's line in Asa di Var goes on: comfort became the disease.

trapdoor: what you thought: religion says suffering is good for you.
what it means: the Gurus call pain a medicine because it wakes a person up, and they never call it sweet.
what a scholar hears: dukh daaroo, sukh rog bhaiaa, in Guru Nanak's Asa di Var, set beside Farid's couplet about the fire in every house.
